items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I talked to Charles about forming a new band... I was still with Charles Lloyd. We were off at that period... we started doing Charles with the quartet... The Charles Lloyd Quartet became a great band that I wanted to stay with.

ctx.x: But go ahead, I worked with him. That’s why I know.

Yeah, Herbie was great man, great bass player too. Herbie had a loft, so a lot of musicians used to go over there play in the lofts all day and all night. Some guys would fall asleep as music would still be going. So it was a very fertile period for the music then. Cecil McBee was in there, and around Slug’s I got to meet people like Hank Mobley, Kenny Dorham, and played with all these people I'd heard and played with on records. Clifford Jordan, I saw Max and Art Blakey and Coltrane. So Tolliver said, "Listen…

Bartz' father's club in Baltimore… we played Slug’s and subsequently actually my first record date was with Jackie but that record, a couple of records didn't come out until after I was with Charles Lloyd. So my first record date was with Jackie. I guess we did one with… we recorded with Bobby Hutcherson and I'm not sure what we did.

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I heard you probably in around 1968 or so, with Charles Lloyd.

ctx.x: I heard you probably in around 1968 or so, with Charles Lloyd. And I’d had a couple of — I’ll call them epiphanies now but that was another one. This was in Rochester in some hall, and I think it was the first time I’d heard drummers and bassists really — I’ll call it playing with the time. Not straight ahead but a little bit of elastic approach to the time.

Well the elastic approach to the time I think I would credit Bill Evans and Paul Motian and Scott LaFaro for that kind of free, open-it-up freedom for each individual to be playing collectively but have an equal input. And so after that “Live at the Village Vanguard” you know it kind of just spread throughout the jazz community. So you know you could break time up. Break it up. And then go into the time later. But for coloring it really opened that up.
